newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Henderson sees HK home prices stabilising.
newsitem.headline: Henderson sees HK home prices stabilising.

text.p: Hong Kong property prices are set to stabilise after a drop of up to 10 percent in resale values since early March, the chairman of major local property developer Henderson Land Development Co Ltd said on Wednesday.

"Property prices in the secondary market have fallen five to 10 percent in April from (their levels) in early March and turnover has been reduced significantly," Lee Shau-kee told Reuters in an interview.
"Prices should stabilise after the recent adjustment."
In a move to curb rising property prices, the government imposed measures last month to increase supply in the territory, extending the pre-sale period for private flats to 15 months from 12 months.

The government also asked property developers to put presale flats onto the market within six months of the government granting approval for them to sell and to release no less than 20 percent of every batch of housing units that is built.

The measures were annnouced the same day that local commercial banks raised their prime lending rate by 25 basis points to 8.75 percent following the U.S. Federal Reserve's first interest rate increase in more than two years.
Analysts said local property prices had surged about 20 percent this year before the market turned quiet in mid-March.
Transactions registered by major property agencies such as Midland Realty and Centaline Property Agency had dropped sharply this month to about one-third of their level in early March, Lee said.
While local developers expressed discontent at government intervention in the property market, Lee said differences between the government and developers were minor.
He said the government had noted that there was a land supply mismatch -- an over-supply of industrial sites but a lack of residential areas.
"The government underestimated citizens' demand for housing units and also failed to predict that a large number of factories would move north into China," Lee said.
Since the government intended to address the problem by changing the purpose of industrial land for residential usage, future home supply should be steady, he added.
"Following the increase of land supply (for housing), the imbalance will be solved and there is no need for further (government) measures," he said.
Lee said Henderson Land had no major property sales scheduled for the coming two months but the company would be guided by market prices when it released new flats for sale.
"If developers just followed the highest price achieved last month, nobody would buy their flats," Lee said, adding that Henderson Land's next major sale would be in June or July.
He said Henderson Land would not bid as aggressively as last year at government land auctions this year due to high prices.
"We were quite aggressive in land auctions before, but we eased off recently due to high prices."

Henderson Land was active in last year's government land auctions, taking up 20 to 30 percent of the amount sold, Lee said. "Even if we do not buy any more land, we still have a big enough land bank for use over the next five years," he added.
